Lessons.Title: Solving Quadratic Equations with the Zero Product Property
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: justify and apply the zero-product property to an expression explicitly equal to zero, solve both linear factors, and check roots without dividing by variable expressions. Original first-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 7 Lesson 4 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/7/4/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/7/4/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source formalizes the reasoning that was previously informal.

Original equation (2x+3)(x−4)=0. Over real numbers, a product is zero if at least one factor is zero: 2x+3=0 yields x=−3/2; x−4=0 yields x=4. Substitution into the original product verifies both. The coefficient2 does not create a third root.

The zero-product property cannot be applied to a product equalling12 as though either factor were12 or0. A nonzero product may have infinitely many factor combinations. Similarly, dividing both sides by x could remove the valid root x0 in an equation with x factor; prefer factoring and check every root.

Student task: illustrate zero products with a numerical table, identify roots for three signed-factor equations, critique a wrong step using zero product for nonzero right side, and explain why every identified root works. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 for property justification, factor equations, root checks and critique of inadmissible transformations.

KeyConcepts.Title: Zero-product property
KeyConcepts.Definition: For real a,b, ab=0 implies a=0 or b=0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear factors
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each factor yields one linear equation to solve.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nonzero product caveat
KeyConcepts.Definition: ab=c with c≠0 does not imply a=0 or b=0.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Bring full expression to zero before using property.

WorkedExamples.Title: Solve two factors
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve(2x+3)(x−4)=0.
WorkedExamples.Method: Solve the original independently authored equation and check every candidate in the source expression.
Steps: Substitute each into its vanishing factor.

WorkedExamples.Title: Show zero-factor identity
WorkedExamples.Question: Why must ab=0 have zero factor over reals?
WorkedExamples.Method: Solve the original independently authored equation and check every candidate in the source expression.
Steps: Suppose neither a nor b is zero.
Then division by a and b is defined and their product is nonzero.
Hence at least one must be zero.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject nonzero misuse
WorkedExamples.Question: Does (x+1)(x+2)=12 imply x=−1 or−2?
WorkedExamples.Method: Solve the original independently authored equation and check every candidate in the source expression.
Steps: Set expression minus12 equal zero before attempting factorization.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; zero-product cannot be applied directly.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying zero product when right side is nonzero
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Factor zero would make left0, not target.

SummaryPoints: A zero product requires at least one zero factor.
Each root must be checked in original expression.
